chapter_theme: Four Patitruppattu fragments outside the surviving tens: the enemies' only choice of tribute before the king's army of thunder, wind, fire and flood; the march that makes kings behind a perfect fort lose heart; three lines of a woman denying another's equality; and the bard who finds the king giving gifts in a war camp that ignores the rains.

fragment:1.reading: The poet asks how enemies could fail to bow, except by heaping rare jewels together with dark-eyed elephants and speaking in submission, before a king whose army spreads like the earth in waves, whose fierce drum roars as the sky shakes when thunder rages, whose vehicles go like the rising wind, whose rage is a fire none can hold, and whose march runs like water racing to the great dark sea.
fragment:1.nuance: The poem gives the enemy only one course: tribute and submissive speech are not one choice among others but the only way to stay unbroken, and the four similes that follow (thunder, wind, fire, water) are the proof. The closing image of the army as land rising in waves turns the solid earth itself into a flood.

thinai_evidence.note: the army's march is described as what forces enemy kings to bow

comparisons.tenor: the war drum roaring with trembling face

fragment:2.reading: The poet tells the king that his march is truly a fine thing here: tuskers with bangled tusks streaming must and digging the earth as they rise, horses crowned with plumes like opening fire and swift as the wind, tall chariots roaring like a waterfall, drums whose faces have received their offering sounding so that the quarters ring, with horn and right-whorled conch blaring, until the kings who would not yield, though their land is guarded by tall walls, rows of battlements, a thorn forest and a deep moat, lose heart, slip from their stand and tremble.
fragment:2.nuance: The enemy's defence is listed in full (wall, battlements, guard forest, moat), and then it fails inside the defenders: the poem places the defeat in their hearts (நெஞ்சுபுகல் அழிந்து) before any assault is described. Line 6's கடுக்கும் is a comparison verb, but what it compares is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the army's march against enemy forts

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the tall chariots

fragment:3.reading: A woman says of another that, though she has a woman's nature of cherished distinction, she is no equal of the speaker, and she knows well enough who her own equals are.
fragment:3.nuance: Three lines without a frame: who speaks and of whom is not given. The measure is rank, not beauty; the speaker grants the other woman her excellence and still denies her equality, and the last line says the other woman knows it herself.

thinai_evidence.note: rivalry between two women is the marutham quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no colophon; the speaker is inferred from the rivalry (a wife about another woman), and the addressee is not known

fragment:4.reading: The bard tells the lord that he has come and has seen him in order to go away rewarded: the king sits in a joyful court giving tuskers, spirited horses, chariots and fine jewels in plenty, does not stop for the rains nor slacken for the cold, keeps an eagerness that the heat of enmity never lets rest, and with his fierce victorious army camped in a foreign land wears down the stand of unyielding warriors, in his boundless camp where must elephants full of strength tear up their posts and roar.
fragment:4.nuance: The gift is given in the war camp, not the capital: the court of laughter (நகைசால் இருக்கை) and the camp of roaring elephants are the same place. The rains and the cold, the seasons that normally halt a campaign, are named only to be ignored.

thinai_evidence.note: the bard praises the king's giving and comes for his gift

links.note: Fragment 1 says enemies cannot escape except by heaping rare jewels with elephants and speaking submissively (யானையொ(டு) அரும்கலம் ... பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல்); Akananuru 124 opens with the same formula (நன்கலம் களிற்றொடு ... வணங்கினர், வழிமொழிந்து) as the condition on which a soldier waiting in camp may go home to his wife.
links.teaches: The submission the praise poet demands as the enemy's only course is, in the akam poem, the event a homesick soldier waits for, so the formula of tribute served both genres and the end of the king's war was imagined from the camp as the start of a lover's return.

links.note: Fragment 1 states as the poet's rhetorical question that enemies have no way but to submit (பணிந்துவழி மொழிதல் அல்லது); Purananuru 17 gives the enemy kings' own words as they decide to submit to the Chera Irumporai for fear of losing their walls and forts.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show that the Chera praise poets treated submission not only as the king's due but as a reasoned choice the enemy makes on seeing his anger, so the boast of the fragment rests on a scene of calculation that Purananuru 17 spells out.

links.note: Kural 744 says a fort is that which destroys the besieging enemy's spirit (உறுபகை ஊக்கம் அழிப்ப தரண்); Fragment 2 lists a fort with tall wall, battlements, guard forest and deep moat and says that it is the defending kings who lose heart (நெஞ்சுபுகல் அழிந்து) at the Chera march.
links.teaches: On the plain reading the two make opposite claims about the same contest of nerve: the Kural gives the fort the power to break the attacker's spirit, while the praise poem says a perfect fort could not keep its own kings' spirit from breaking, so the war of morale the Kural assigns to walls the poet assigns to the king's army.

links.note: Fragment 3 has a woman say that another, for all her excellence, is not her equal and knows who her equals are (என்னொடு புரையுநள் அல்லள்); Ainkurunuru 67, a wife's speech in marutham, says the hero's new woman, foolish, sets herself against the wife who is no match for her (தன்னொடு நிகரா என்னொடு நிகரி).
links.teaches: Ainkurunuru 67 supplies the frame the three-line fragment lacks: claims of who is whose equal are the weapon of the marutham quarrel between wife and new woman, which makes it likely the fragment is such a speech and that its point is standing in the household rather than beauty.

links.note: Fragment 4 has the bard come to see the king (வந்தனென் பெரும கண்டனென்) in his camp with the army camped in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்(து) இறுத்த ... தானையொடு), where elephants full of strength (மைந்துமலி) tear up their posts; Purananuru 22 ends with the poet come to see the Chera Irumporai (வந்து இனிது காண்டிசின்) with his army camping in foreign land (வேறுபுலத்து இறுக்கும் தானையோடு) and opens with strong elephants (மைந்து மலிந்த மழ களிறு) standing at their posts.
links.teaches: The shared phrases show that the bard's visit to a Chera king in his foreign war camp was a set scene with its own diction, and the one change, elephants standing quiet at the post in Purananuru 22 against elephants tearing the post up in the fragment, turns the same scene from settled order to war still pending.

links.note: Kural 610 says a king without sloth (மடியிலா மன்னவன்) gains the whole earth; Fragment 4 praises a king who does not stop for the rains nor slacken for the cold (பனிஎன மடியாய்) and keeps his army in foreign land.
links.teaches: The Kural states freedom from sloth as a ruler's general virtue, while the fragment shows what it meant in war: refusing the seasonal halt of the rains and the cold that normally ended a campaign, so the king's tirelessness was measured against the calendar of war.

source_issues: fragment:1-4: no colophon (thinai, thurai, poet, patron all null); no decade or king is named, so the thinai here is inferred from the lines alone.
fragment:1 line 7: repaired TSCII leftover for ரி (flag); எரிநிகழ்ந் தன்ன reads well.
fragment:1 line 6: ஊர்திக் கால்முளை is obscure (கால் as wheel or wind, முளை unclear); the reading takes only the simile of the wind.
fragment:1 line 10: நிலந்திரைப் பன்ன is split oddly; read as நிலம் திரைப்ப அன்ன, the land rising in waves.
fragment:2 line 2: நிலம்புடையூ looks like a damaged form (புடையூஉ?); line 5-6 (கோன்முனைக் கொடியினம் விரவா வல்லோ(டு) ஊன்வினை கடுக்குந் தோன்றல) and line 8 (கண்வேட் டனவே) are obscure.
fragment:3: three lines with no frame, and a love speech in a book of royal praise; the speaker is not given.
fragment:4 line 10: இடாஅ ஏணிநின் is run together; read as இடாஅ ஏணி நின் (your boundless camp).
Bracketed letters in all four fragments (யானையொ(டு), விசும்(பு)) are the edition's marking of elided letters; forms are copied with them.
